transitivity: both — transitive (gas distends the stomach), intransitive (her abdomen distended)
gloss: To swell outward from pressure inside, or to make something swell that way.
examples: Too much air will *distend* the tissue.
Her stomach *distended* painfully after the meal.
The vet found a *distended* loop of intestine.

gloss: To purify a liquid by boiling and condensing it, or to reduce something to its essential part.
examples: They *distill* the whiskey twice before bottling it.
She *distilled* three hundred pages into a single chart.
The findings have been *distilled* into one page.
contrast: American English writes distill, British distil with one -l. Both double the l before -ed and -ing: distilled, distilling.

transitivity: both — transitive (distort the facts), intransitive (the sound distorts at high volume)
gloss: To twist something out of its true shape, sound, or meaning.
examples: Cheap lenses *distort* straight lines.
The article *distorted* what she actually said.
His voice was *distorted* by the bad connection.

gloss: To hesitate and delay instead of making a decision.
examples: Do not *dither* — the offer expires tonight.
The committee *dithered* for months over the budget.
While they were *dithering*, a rival bought the company.

gloss: To separate and go in different directions, or to differ from something.
examples: The two trails *diverge* just past the bridge.
Their opinions *diverged* sharply after the vote.
Our careers had *diverged* long before graduation.
contrast: Diverge takes from: the results diverge from earlier findings.

transitivity: both — transitive (divest its holdings), intransitive (divest from coal)
gloss: To sell off a business or investment, or to strip someone of something they hold.
examples: The university plans to *divest* from fossil fuels.
The company *divested* its European division last year.
He was *divested* of his title after the scandal.
contrast: Divest takes of when someone is stripped of something and from when an investor sells out: divested of his rank, divested from oil.

gloss: To work out or guess something hidden without direct evidence.
examples: Analysts try to *divine* the bank's next move.
She *divined* from his tone that something was wrong.
No one has *divined* the author's real intent.
contrast: Spelled and pronounced exactly like the adjective divine (божественный), but the verb means to guess something hidden.

gloss: To reveal information that was supposed to stay secret.
examples: The company refuses to *divulge* the terms of the deal.
He *divulged* the password to a stranger.
Nothing has been *divulged* about the investigation.

gloss: To change something dishonestly, especially a document, a photo, or a drink.
examples: It is a crime to *doctor* official records.
Someone *doctored* the photo before posting it.
The books had been *doctored* to hide the losses.
contrast: Same word as the noun doctor (врач), but the verb means to tamper with something.

gloss: To follow or trouble someone persistently.
examples: Money problems *dog* the project at every stage.
Injuries *dogged* him throughout the season.
The scandal has *dogged* the mayor for years.
contrast: One syllable ending in a single consonant, so the g doubles: dogged, dogging.

gloss: To make someone or something certain to fail or suffer.
examples: One bad decision can *doom* an entire campaign.
The leak *doomed* their chances of winning.
The plan was *doomed* from the start.
contrast: Doom takes to: doomed to failure, doomed to repeat it.

transitivity: both — transitive (dope the horse), intransitive (athletes who dope)
gloss: To give someone drugs secretly, or to take banned performance drugs in sport.
examples: A few riders still *dope* to gain an edge.
The trainer *doped* two of the horses.
He admits he was *doping* all season.
contrast: Drop the silent -e before -ed and -ing: dope → doped, doping.

gloss: To mark something with dots, or to be scattered all over a surface.
examples: Small farms *dot* the valley floor.
She *dotted* the map with red pins.
The hills are *dotted* with wind turbines.
contrast: One syllable, one vowel, one final consonant, so the t doubles: dotted, dotting.

transitivity: both — intransitive (the plans dovetail), transitive (dovetail the schedules)
gloss: To fit together neatly with something else.
examples: Her research and his *dovetail* almost perfectly.
The new rules *dovetailed* with existing state law.
We are *dovetailing* the two schedules this week.
contrast: Dovetail takes with: the findings dovetail with earlier work.

gloss: To knock something down, or to swallow a drink or food quickly.
examples: High winds can *down* power lines in seconds.
He *downed* the coffee and ran for the bus.
Three trees were *downed* by the storm.

gloss: To make something seem less important or serious than it really is.
examples: Officials tend to *downplay* early warnings.
She *downplayed* her role in the discovery.
The risks were *downplayed* in the summary.
contrast: Vowel + -y, so the y stays: downplays, downplayed, never downplaid.

transitivity: both — transitive (downsize the staff), intransitive (the company downsized)
gloss: To reduce the size of a company or a household, usually by cutting jobs or moving somewhere smaller.
examples: Firms *downsize* when orders dry up.
The plant *downsized* twice in three years.
Her whole department was *downsized* last spring.
contrast: Drop the silent -e before -ing: downsize → downsizing.

gloss: To vote against a post or comment online so that its score goes down.
examples: Readers *downvote* anything that looks like an ad.
Someone *downvoted* every answer in the thread.
His question was *downvoted* within minutes.
contrast: Drop the silent -e before -ing: downvote → downvoting. The opposite is upvote.

transitivity: both — intransitive (he drawls a little), transitive (drawl an answer)
gloss: To speak slowly, stretching the vowels out.
examples: People from that part of Texas *drawl* a little.
'Take your time,' he *drawled*.
She was *drawling* her words on purpose.

gloss: To clear mud and silt from the bottom of a river or harbor, or to drag something up from it.
examples: The city plans to *dredge* the shipping channel.
Crews *dredged* the lake for the missing boat.
The harbor has not been *dredged* since 2009.
contrast: Drop the silent -e before -ing: dredge → dredging.

gloss: To make a low continuous humming sound, or to speak in a dull monotonous voice.
examples: Air conditioners *drone* all summer here.
The engine *droned* for hours.
He was *droning* through forty slides.
contrast: Drop the silent -e before -ed and -ing: droned, droning.

gloss: To bend or hang down from weakness, tiredness, or weight.
examples: The flowers *droop* if you forget to water them.
His eyelids *drooped* halfway through the lecture.
The flag was *drooping* in the still air.

gloss: To give someone drugs, usually secretly, to make them sleepy or unconscious.
examples: Thieves sometimes *drug* a victim's drink.
Someone *drugged* the guard dogs.
She believes she was *drugged* at the party.
contrast: One syllable ending in a single consonant, so the g doubles: drugged, drugging.

ru: чистить в химчистке, отдавать в химчистку
gloss: To clean clothes with chemicals instead of water.
examples: You have to *dry-clean* a wool coat.
I *dry-cleaned* the suit before the interview.
The curtains are being *dry-cleaned* this week.
contrast: The verb keeps its hyphen: dry-clean, dry-cleaned. The shop is a dry cleaner's, two words.

gloss: To fight or compete one against one.
examples: The two aces *duel* again tonight.
They *dueled* over the amendment for weeks.
The candidates have been *dueling* on television all month.
contrast: American English keeps one l — dueled, dueling — while British writes duelled, duelling. Sounds the same as the adjective dual (двойной).

transitivity: both — transitive (dull the pain), intransitive (the colors dulled)
gloss: To make something less sharp, bright, or intense, or to become so.
examples: Two aspirin will *dull* the pain for a while.
The paint *dulled* after a single winter.
Years of routine had *dulled* his curiosity.

gloss: To astonish someone so much that they cannot speak.
examples: Results like that *dumbfound* the experts.
The verdict *dumbfounded* everyone in the courtroom.
She was *dumbfounded* by the size of the offer.
contrast: The b is silent, as in dumb: dum-FOWND. The spelling dumfound also exists, but dumbfound is the usual American form.

gloss: To trick someone into believing or doing something.
examples: Fake sites *dupe* thousands of shoppers a year.
He *duped* investors out of millions.
They were *duped* into signing away their rights.
contrast: Drop the silent -e before -ed and -ing: dupe → duped, duping.

gloss: To make something else look small by comparison.
examples: The new tower will *dwarf* every building nearby.
This year's losses *dwarfed* last year's.
The stage was *dwarfed* by the size of the crowd.

gloss: To blow something up with dynamite.
examples: Engineers had to *dynamite* the old dam.
They *dynamited* the roadblock at dawn.
The tunnel was *dynamited* shut.
contrast: Drop the silent -e before -ed and -ing: dynamited, dynamiting.

gloss: To set money or resources aside for one specific purpose.
examples: Congress may *earmark* funds for rural clinics.
The city *earmarked* two million dollars for repairs.
That land has been *earmarked* for housing.
contrast: Earmark takes for: earmarked for research.

transitivity: both — intransitive (edge toward the door), transitive (edge the lawn)
gloss: To move little by little in one direction, or to form a border along something.
examples: Prices *edge* higher every month.
He *edged* toward the exit without a word.
She was *edging* along the narrow ledge.
contrast: Drop the silent -e before -ing: edge → edging.

gloss: To mix personal opinion into what is supposed to be a factual report.
examples: Reporters should not *editorialize* in a news story.
The anchor *editorialized* about the mayor for two minutes.
Critics said the paper was *editorializing* on its front page.
contrast: American spelling ends in -ize; British writes editorialise.

gloss: To bring something about, especially a change.
examples: Only Congress can *effect* a change this large.
The new director *effected* a complete turnaround.
Reforms have been *effected* at every level.
contrast: Do not confuse with affect. To affect something is to influence it; to effect something is to make it happen. Effect is usually the noun (эффект) and only rarely this verb.

gloss: To supply something with electric power, or to excite a crowd suddenly.
examples: The state plans to *electrify* the whole rail line.
Her performance *electrified* the audience.
The village was *electrified* only in 1974.
contrast: Consonant + -y: electrifies, electrified, but electrifying keeps the y.

gloss: To kill or badly injure someone with an electric shock.
examples: A downed line can *electrocute* anyone who touches it.
The fault nearly *electrocuted* a technician.
Two workers were *electrocuted* at the site.

gloss: To draw a response, answer, or reaction out of someone.
examples: Good questions *elicit* honest answers.
The ad *elicited* hundreds of complaints.
So far the letter has *elicited* no response.
contrast: Do not confuse with the adjective illicit (незаконный), which sounds almost identical.

transitivity: both — transitive (elongate the shape), intransitive (the shadows elongate)
gloss: To make something longer, or to grow longer.
examples: Heels *elongate* the line of the leg.
The shadows *elongated* as the sun dropped.
The cells become *elongated* as they mature.

transitivity: both — transitive (elucidate the point), intransitive (he declined to elucidate)
gloss: To make something clear by explaining it carefully.
examples: The footnotes *elucidate* the author's sources.
She *elucidated* the theory with a simple diagram.
The paper has *elucidated* a mechanism no one understood.

gloss: To escape or avoid someone, or to stay beyond someone's reach or understanding.
examples: The right word can *elude* you for hours.
The suspect *eluded* police for a week.
The prize has *eluded* her three years running.
contrast: Do not confuse with allude (to mention indirectly): he alluded to the problem, but a solution eluded him.

transitivity: both — intransitive (light emanates from it), transitive (she emanates calm)
gloss: To come out from a source, or to give off a quality or feeling.
examples: Strange noises *emanate* from the basement at night.
A faint smell of smoke *emanated* from the kitchen.
The order turned out to have *emanated* from the mayor's office.
contrast: Emanate takes from: the light emanates from a single bulb.

gloss: To free someone from slavery, legal control, or restriction.
examples: The bill would *emancipate* minors at sixteen.
Lincoln *emancipated* the slaves in 1863.
She was legally *emancipated* at seventeen.

gloss: To treat a dead body with chemicals so that it does not decay.
examples: Funeral homes *embalm* most bodies before a viewing.
The Egyptians *embalmed* their kings.
Lenin's body was *embalmed* and put on display.
contrast: The l is silent, as in calm and palm: im-BAHM.

gloss: To ban trade in something, or to forbid the release of news until a set time.
examples: Several states want to *embargo* the chemical.
Washington *embargoed* Cuban sugar in 1960.
The report is *embargoed* until Monday morning.
contrast: Ends in -o, so the third person adds -es: embargoes, embargoed.

gloss: To display a name, design, or slogan prominently on something.
examples: Teams *emblazon* the sponsor's name across the chest.
They *emblazoned* the logo on every window.
His face was *emblazoned* on a million posters.
contrast: Emblazon takes on or with: emblazoned on the door, emblazoned with a crest.

gloss: To be a clear example or physical expression of an idea or quality.
examples: Few leaders *embody* the values they preach.
That building *embodied* everything wrong with the era.
The rules are *embodied* in a single statute.
contrast: Consonant + -y: embodies, embodied, but embodying keeps the y.

gloss: To press a raised design or lettering into a surface.
examples: They can *emboss* your initials on the cover.
The printer *embossed* the invitations in gold.
Each card is *embossed* with the bank's crest.
contrast: Ends in -ss, so the third person adds -es: embosses.

gloss: To involve someone deeply in an argument or a difficult situation.
examples: One careless email can *embroil* a whole department.
The deal *embroiled* the firm in a two-year lawsuit.
He is *embroiled* in a fight with his own party.
contrast: Embroil takes in: embroiled in a scandal.

transitivity: both — transitive (emcee the show), intransitive (he emcees for a living)
gloss: To act as the host who introduces the acts or speakers at an event.
examples: A local comedian will *emcee* the awards.
She *emceed* the benefit two years running.
He has been *emceeing* weddings since college.
contrast: Spelled out from the letters M.C. (master of ceremonies): emcees, emceed, emceeing.

ru: бурно выражать чувства, играть с чувством
gloss: To show emotion openly, often in an exaggerated or theatrical way.
examples: Some actors *emote* far too much on camera.
He *emoted* through the entire second act.
She was *emoting* for the cameras.
contrast: Drop the silent -e before -ed and -ing: emoted, emoting.

transitivity: both — transitive (emulsify the butter), intransitive (the sauce emulsifies)
gloss: To mix two liquids that normally separate, such as oil and water, into one smooth blend.
examples: Whisk the oil in slowly to *emulsify* the dressing.
The sauce *emulsified* as soon as I added the yolk.
Keep *emulsifying* until it thickens.
contrast: Consonant + -y: emulsifies, emulsified, but emulsifying keeps the y.

gloss: To fill someone with love or admiration, most often used in the passive.
examples: The film tries to *enamor* the audience with nostalgia.
The city *enamored* her from the first day.
He is not *enamored* of the new schedule.
contrast: American spelling enamor, British enamour. It usually appears in the passive with of or with: enamored of the idea.

ru: кратко выражать, резюмировать; заключать в оболочку
gloss: To express the essence of something briefly, or to enclose it in a protective shell.
examples: One photo can *encapsulate* an entire war.
Her answer *encapsulated* the whole problem.
The chips are *encapsulated* in resin.

gloss: To cover or enclose something completely in a surrounding material.
examples: Builders *encase* the steel in concrete.
Ice *encased* every branch by morning.
The engine is *encased* in a soundproof box.
contrast: Encase takes in: encased in glass. Drop the silent -e before -ing: encasing.

gloss: To form a circle around something or someone.
examples: A high wall *encircles* the old town.
Troops *encircled* the city within a day.
The lake is *encircled* by pines.

gloss: To put information into a code or a particular form, as in computing or genetics.
examples: The app will *encode* the file before sending it.
They *encoded* the message with a simple cipher.
This gene *encodes* a protein that repairs damage.
contrast: Drop the silent -e before -ing: encode → encoding. The opposite is decode.

gloss: To include or cover a wide range of things.
examples: The term *encompasses* far more than software.
The survey *encompassed* twelve states.
The park was expanded to *encompass* the wetlands.
contrast: Ends in -ss, so the third person adds -es: encompasses.

gloss: To move gradually into someone else's space, time, or rights.
examples: New subdivisions *encroach* on the forest every year.
Work *encroached* on every weekend that spring.
The desert has been *encroaching* for decades.
contrast: Encroach takes on or upon: encroach on his rights. Third person adds -es: encroaches.

gloss: To try hard to do something.
examples: We *endeavor* to answer every message within a day.
She *endeavored* to keep her voice steady.
They have *endeavored* to settle the case quietly.
contrast: American spelling endeavor, British endeavour. It takes a to-infinitive: endeavor to explain.
